}","[H-1] Redemption Fee Mechanism Creates Uncollateralized YUSD, Leading to De-Peg When a user redeems YUSD, the `approveRedeemRequest` function first sends the user the full collateral amount that backed the initial mint. Only after this transfer does it take a fee from the user's YUSD, sending it to an insurance fund and burning the remainder. The critical flaw is that the YUSD sent as a fee is now uncollateralized, as its backing assets have already been given to the redeeming user. This uncollateralized YUSD remains in circulation and can be redeemed by others, draining the protocol's reserves. Over time, this will inevitably lead to the insolvency and de-pegging of the YUSD stablecoin.  [M-1] Collateral Can Become Stuck or Mistaken for Protocol Profit he protocol's design involves moving collateral from custodial partners to the `AegisMinting` contract just in time to fulfill redemption requests. However, if a redemption request is canceled or rejected after the collateral has been moved, there is no mechanism to send these funds back to the custodial partners, causing them to become stuck . Furthermore, a separate `depositIncome` function could misinterpret this stuck collateral as protocol profit and mint new, uncollateralized YUSD against it, further destabilizing the peg.

[M-2] Redemption Limit Can Be Exploited to Cause Denial of Service A malicious whale can grief the protocol by consuming the entire periodic redemption limit with requests and then canceling them. Because the limit is not credited back upon cancellation, this creates a Denial of Service, blocking all legitimate users from redeeming their YUSD for the duration of the period.",7587,835,"pragma solidity 0.8.26
